html:
The making of Japan's first constitution, proclaimed on 11 February 1889, on the model of the Prussian and German constitutions. The Meiji Constitution stayed in force until 1947.

After the Meiji Restoration, Japan's leaders wanted a constitution to look modern to the Western powers, but not one that gave power to parliament. In 1882 Itō Hirobumi went to Europe to study. In Berlin and Vienna he learned from the legal scholars Rudolf von Gneist and Lorenz von Stein, and he admired the system Bismarck ran in Germany, where a strong monarch kept control of the army and the cabinet. A German adviser, Hermann Roesler, helped draft the text.

The result made the emperor sovereign and set up an elected lower house with limited powers. The army answered to the emperor, not to the cabinet, a gap that let military leaders take over in the 1930s. The postwar Constitution of Japan replaced it.
